subject: Urology
title: Urolithiasis
subtitle: Epidemiology, stone composition, renal colic, investigations, management, procedures, bladder stones and prevention
sourceNote: Built only from the uploaded Urolithiasis / Urinary Stones lecture by Dr Amr Hassan Alkhalily. The bank preserves the lecture terminology, percentages, imaging statements, management thresholds and referral criteria without adding external guideline updates.

cases.title: Classical Ureteric Colic
cases.scenario: A patient develops sudden severe flank pain radiating to the ipsilateral groin with nausea, vomiting and haematuria.
questions: What is the most likely diagnosis?
List the immediate analgesic options in the lecture.
answer: Ureteric colic due to an obstructing ureteric stone.
Acute loin-to-groin pain, nausea and vomiting, and haematuria.
Obstruction raises collecting-system intraluminal pressure and stretches nerve endings; inflammatory mediators, oedema and hyperperistalsis also contribute.
NSAIDs; morphine or pethidine may be required.
cases.memory: Loin to groin + vomiting + haematuria = ureteric colic.

cases.title: Distal Ureteric Stone
cases.scenario: A stone becomes lodged in the distal ureter or intramural tunnel.
questions: What irritative urinary symptoms may occur?
answer: Because the distal stone irritates the bladder mucosa.
cases.memory: Distal stone irritates bladder: frequency, urgency, testicular/groin pain.

cases.title: Fever with Obstructed Kidney
cases.scenario: A patient with a ureteric stone has fever and urinary obstruction.
questions: What is the required immediate principle of management?
Is this an indication for immediate urological referral?
answer: Urgent decompression of the collecting system.
Yes; sepsis or UTI with obstructive uropathy requires immediate referral.
cases.memory: Fever + obstruction = infected obstructed kidney = urgent decompression.

cases.title: Recurrent UTI with Staghorn Stone
cases.scenario: A patient has recurrent upper urinary tract infections and a branching renal stone.
questions: What stone type is most likely?
State its urine pH and radiological character.
answer: It forms in alkaline urine and is radio-opaque.
Urease-producing organisms split urea, forming ammonium.
cases.memory: Urease infection -> alkaline urine -> struvite -> staghorn.

cases.title: Radiolucent Stone in Acidic Urine
cases.scenario: A patient has a stone not seen on plain KUB and acidic urine.
questions: What percentage of stone types does it represent in the lecture?
What medical dissolution option is stated?
answer: Oral alkalinizing agents can dissolve it.
cases.memory: Uric acid: radiolucent, acidic urine, alkalinize to dissolve.

cases.title: Stable Asymptomatic Calyceal Stone
cases.scenario: An asymptomatic calyceal stone has remained stable for six months.
questions: Is treatment of all renal stones considered settled?
answer: No; the lecture states that treating all renal stones remains debatable.
cases.memory: Stable asymptomatic calyceal stone for 6 months -> annual follow-up may suffice.

cases.title: Renal Stone 1.5 cm
cases.scenario: A patient has a 1.5 cm renal stone.
questions: Which two active treatment options are stated for this size?
answer: ESWL or flexible ureteroscopy with laser disintegration.
A renal stone under 2 cm in a patent urinary tract is suitable for ESWL.
PCNL is used for a stone larger than 2 cm.
cases.memory: 1-2 cm: ESWL or flexible URS; >2 cm: PCNL.

cases.title: Large Renal Stone
questions: What is the preferred modality in the lecture?

cases.title: Obstruction in a Solitary Kidney
cases.scenario: A patient with a solitary functioning kidney has unilateral stone obstruction and acute kidney injury.
questions: Which emergency indication does this represent?
answer: Unilateral obstruction with AKI in a solitary functioning kidney.
Immediate urological referral and urgent decompression.
cases.memory: Solitary kidney + obstruction + AKI = urgent decompression.

cases.title: Persistent Ureteric Stone over 10 mm
cases.scenario: An adult has a ureteric stone larger than 10 mm without sepsis.
questions: Which modality is shown for stones above 10 mm in the lecture flowchart?
answer: Yes; ureteral stones >10 mm are an indication for surgical management.
Failed observation in pregnancy, persistent kidney obstruction related to stones, and recurrent UTI related to stones.
cases.memory: Ureteral stone >10 mm -> intervention; flowchart points to URS.

cases.title: Bladder Stone
cases.scenario: A pelvic X-ray demonstrates a large bladder stone.
questions: State the two treatment options in the lecture.
answer: The stone is broken and removed using a cystoscope.
cases.memory: Bladder stone: cystolitholapaxy; open cystolithotomy if needed.

cases.title: Recurrent Stone Former
cases.scenario: A treated patient asks how to reduce recurrence.
questions: How common is recurrence according to the lecture?
What monitoring is mentioned with citrate?
answer: Nearly half develop a second stone within 5-7 years.
Plenty of fluid throughout the day; balanced diet high in fibre and vegetables, with normal calcium and limited sodium and animal protein.
Thiazide diuretics, allopurinol and citrate supplementation.
Monitor potassium levels and liver enzymes.
cases.memory: Prevent recurrence: fluids all day, normal calcium, less salt/animal protein.

coreShorts.a: Nearly half develop a second stone within 5-7 years.

coreShorts.q: How does urine composition relate to stone composition?
coreShorts.a: Higher urinary concentrations of calcium, oxalate or uric acid favour corresponding stone formation.
